outcome: labour cost stays inside the weekly budget
problem: Swaps are approved without any view of the worker's running weekly hours, so overtime is only discovered at payroll.
scenarios: Approved three trades on Friday and found out Monday that Dmitri ended at 52 hours; finance flagged it.
Our Q3 spend at Dock 4 was 9% over plan because of trades nobody checked.
I want a heads-up before I click yes on a trade, not a report after the pay run.
Leads approve trades from the floor in ten seconds; nobody can add up hours in their head.
statement: Warehouse shift leads need to see before approving a swap whether it pushes someone into overtime so that labour cost stays inside the weekly budget

outcome: residents see familiar carers and agency spend falls
problem: Vacancies are broadcast to everyone at once, so agency nurses take shifts that in-house bank staff would have covered.
scenarios: Mrs Okafor's dementia wing had four unknown faces last week and two families complained.
Outside-supplier invoices hit £38k in March while our bank team sat at home.
The vacancy blast goes to everybody and the agency nurses grab them in minutes.
I want my in-house bank to get a two-hour head start on any gap.
statement: Care home rota managers need to offer open shifts to their own float pool before agency staff so that residents see familiar carers and agency spend falls

outcome: extra hours follow the collective agreement and avoid grievances
problem: Open shifts go to whoever taps first, which breaks union contracts that allocate extra work by length of service.
scenarios: Local 418 filed a grievance because a six-month picker got Saturday OT before a 12-year guy.
Our contract says spare work goes by hire date; the app hands it to the fastest thumb.
The steward wants proof of who was asked first and in which sequence.
We still run a paper sign-up sheet by the time clock because the app can't do it right.
statement: Unionised warehouse supervisors need to offer open shifts in seniority order so that extra hours follow the collective agreement and avoid grievances

outcome: every client post is covered and guards know where they are going
problem: A shift is tied to one location, so guards who move between client buildings are tracked in side spreadsheets.
scenarios: One shift on paper is really four hours at Lakeside Tower then four at the bus depot.
We keep a second spreadsheet of posts because the rota only knows 'Northgate - Day'.
A customer phoned at 2am asking why reception was empty; the officer was at the other building.
Supervisors text the location list to the team every morning.
statement: Security operations managers need to schedule guards who rotate across several client sites in one shift so that every client post is covered and guards know where they are going

outcome: an empty post is spotted before the client notices
problem: Supervisors cannot see in real time which gates and lobbies are staffed, so gaps are found by complaints.
scenarios: At 3am I have no idea which gates are actually staffed right now.
Lost the Brennan Logistics contract after their gatehouse sat unmanned for 40 minutes.
I want a wall screen with every gate and lobby, green or red.
Phoning six officers to find out who's where takes my whole night.
statement: Security supervisors need to see live coverage per client post across all sites so that an empty post is spotted before the client notices

outcome: they arrange renewals before nurses lose placements
problem: Coordinators only discover expiring certificates when a hospital turns a nurse away.
scenarios: Lost a two-week ICU block at St. Bride's because Amaka's BLS ran out the day before.
I pull a monthly report from three systems to know who needs a CPR refresher.
We find out about an expired card when the ward refuses the nurse at the door.
I'd book the refresher class if I just knew who was due.
statement: Agency placement coordinators need to see which nurses' credentials lapse in the next 60 days so that they arrange renewals before nurses lose placements

outcome: nobody turns up an hour early or late
problem: Recurring shifts are stored in one timezone offset, so they move by an hour at daylight-saving changes in some states.
scenarios: Half the Sunday night crew showed up at 9 instead of 10.
Everything in the app is suddenly off by an hour, and only for the Phoenix site.
My schedule said 6am, I came at 6, the lead says I'm late.
Since last weekend the rota and the time clock disagree.
statement: Multi-state ops admins need to keep recurring shifts at the same local clock time across daylight-saving changes so that nobody turns up an hour early or late

outcome: staffing matches the trucks actually arriving
problem: Headcount is guessed from last week's rota while the WMS already knows how many trailers are booked.
scenarios: Tuesday we had 40 pickers and 6 trailers; Thursday 22 pickers and 19 trailers.
I copy pallet counts from Manhattan into Excel and then guess headcount.
Overstaffed Monday, sending people home early, and they hate it.
Promo week caught us short again because nobody looked at the ASN list.
statement: Warehouse planners need to build next week's rota from inbound volume forecasts so that staffing matches the trucks actually arriving

outcome: they never spend time building schedules
problem: Building rotas is manual work every week, and admins want it fully handed off.
scenarios: Why do I still drag blocks around in 2026? Let the AI do it and send it out.
A competitor demoed one button that makes the whole month.
I lose every Thursday afternoon to the plan for 30 couriers.
Make it like autopilot, I'll fix the odd mistake after.
statement: Ops admins need to have rotas generated and published automatically without a manager so that they never spend time building schedules

outcome: they are only offered visits they can actually do
problem: Availability is one fixed weekly pattern, so aides with alternating custody or second jobs get booked on days they can't work.
scenarios: I have my kids every other week, so I can only work weekends on odd weeks.
The coordinator keeps booking me Tuesdays when I told her I can't.
The availability screen only lets me pick one fixed week.
I've turned down six calls this month because they landed on my custody days.
statement: Home care aides need to set availability that alternates week by week so that they are only offered visits they can actually do

outcome: they can plan childcare and second jobs months ahead
problem: Shifts change every week, so workers with outside commitments cannot plan and leave.
scenarios: At my old DC we bid on lines every three months; here it changes weekly.
I work at a gym too, I need to know my nights for the whole season.
Supervisors spend days on a paper bid sheet.
People quit because they can't plan anything.
statement: Distribution centre staff need to bid on fixed shift patterns each quarter so that they can plan childcare and second jobs months ahead

outcome: forklift and reach-truck lines are never run by untrained staff
problem: The rota has no notion of station skills, so untrained people are placed on equipment.
scenarios: The rota put a temp on the high-bay picker; he'd never touched one.
We track who's signed off on what on a whiteboard in the break room.
Safety officer wants the schedule to refuse to place Jo on the FLT until she's certified.
Monday we had 5 pickers and no one who could run the packing machine.
statement: Fulfilment shift leads need to assign people only to stations they are trained on so that forklift and reach-truck lines are never run by untrained staff

outcome: setting up a new contract takes minutes not days
problem: Each new building's rota has to be built by hand even when every site has the same pattern.
scenarios: We won 28 office blocks for Calder Bank and I'm building each evening rota by hand.
Every site is basically 6pm-10pm, three cleaners, and I click it 28 times.
Onboarding the Metro Transit stations will take me two weeks of data entry.
Can I just clone the Wexford site and change the address?
statement: Regional cleaning managers need to copy a shift template across dozens of client buildings so that setting up a new contract takes minutes not days

outcome: standby and callouts are tracked without a spreadsheet
problem: On-call cover can only be entered as a normal shift, which counts as worked hours and distorts overtime.
scenarios: Our nurses carry the pager every fifth weekend and it lives in a Google Sheet.
If I enter on-call as a normal block it counts as hours and breaks overtime.
Payroll asks me every month who got called in at night.
We need standby that's visible but isn't a real duty.
statement: Clinic managers need to run an on-call rota separate from worked shifts so that standby and callouts are tracked without a spreadsheet

outcome: routes leave on time when someone calls in sick
problem: Same-day gaps are filled by phoning drivers one by one, and many drivers don't use the app.
scenarios: 6:10am, two out sick, I'm ringing people one by one with 40 parcels sitting.
Our WhatsApp group is how we fill gaps and it's chaos.
Some of our drivers don't have the app, just a phone that gets texts.
Vans left 50 minutes late Tuesday because I couldn't find cover.
statement: Courier depot managers need to fill a same-day gap by texting available drivers in one go so that routes leave on time when someone calls in sick

outcome: the warehouse has enough hands for holiday volume
problem: Any supervisor can approve leave in the busiest weeks, and planners only find out when the peak rota is short.
scenarios: Twelve pickers got approved for Thanksgiving week by a new supervisor.
Every October I have to tell people their approved leave is cancelled.
Can the app just refuse leave from Nov 20 to Dec 24?
We were 30% short on Cyber Monday because of approved vacations.
statement: Peak-season planners need to block time-off requests during the November-December peak so that the warehouse has enough hands for holiday volume

outcome: carers spend their time with clients, not in traffic
problem: Visit runs are planned without any map, so carers zigzag across town.
scenarios: My carer had back-to-back calls on opposite ends of Leeds with 15 minutes in between.
We plan the day on a paper map with pins.
A competitor has a map that orders the calls for you.
Staff are burning petrol and arriving late to Mrs Hale every day.
statement: Home care schedulers need to build visit runs that keep travel between clients short so that carers spend their time with clients, not in traffic

outcome: shifts fill hours earlier and fewer go unfilled
problem: Nurses learn about available shifts and their pay only by phoning the agency, so fills are slow.
scenarios: Nurses ring me at 7am asking what's on today and I read the list out.
Every nurse asks me what it pays before saying yes.
By the time I've phoned around, a rival agency has taken it.
Vantor won't sign unless their people can self-book.
statement: Staffing agency coordinators need to publish client hospital shifts to their nurse pool with rates shown so that shifts fill hours earlier and fewer go unfilled

outcome: staff without smartphones still know their hours
problem: The only printable view cuts off long rotas, and many cleaners never open the app.
scenarios: Half my team are 60+ and don't use the app; they look at the wall.
The PDF cuts off after 12 names.
I screenshot the schedule and paste it into Word every Friday.
Need something A4 I can pin up in the laundry room.
statement: Cleaning site supervisors need to print a weekly rota for the noticeboard so that staff without smartphones still know their hours

outcome: one depot's quiet day covers another's rush without new hires
problem: Each site's rota is isolated, so borrowed staff can't be scheduled or clock in at the other site.
scenarios: Leeds was idle Tuesday while Bradford was 8 short, 12 miles apart.
Borrowed staff don't show on the other site's rota, so they can't punch in there.
I arrange it by phone and payroll charges the wrong cost centre.
Ironvale wants to share pickers across the Midlands hubs.
statement: Regional logistics managers need to lend workers between nearby depots for a day so that one depot's quiet day covers another's rush without new hires

outcome: they stop overspending before the week starts
problem: Labour budgets live in finance spreadsheets, so managers only learn about overspend weeks later.
scenarios: Finance tells me three weeks later that Week 32 was £14k over.
I'd cut an evening slot if I could see the money while I plan.
Our hours plan lives in a separate spreadsheet nobody updates.
The area director wants a red flag when a site's rota exceeds plan.
statement: Site general managers need to see scheduled labour cost against budget while editing the rota so that they stop overspending before the week starts

outcome: simple swaps don't wait days for approval
problem: Every like-for-like swap needs a manager's click, so swaps happen off the system.
scenarios: Two seniors want to trade a Sunday and I'm on holiday, so it sits pending.
Staff sort it out on WhatsApp and then the rota is wrong.
Every trade between two qualified seniors needs my click; it's silly.
By the time I approve, the shift's already happened.
statement: Care home managers need to let carers swap shifts directly when both hold the same role so that simple swaps don't wait days for approval

outcome: big events are covered without building every shift by hand
problem: The product assumes a stable weekly roster, so festivals and concerts are planned in Excel.
scenarios: The stadium concert Saturday needs 220 stewards in 9 roles; I'm doing that in Excel.
Apex won't move to Crewday unless we can run a festival weekend.
I hire 80 casuals for one night; they shouldn't need full onboarding.
For each gig I recreate the same layout of gates and bars.
statement: Event security managers need to staff one-off events with hundreds of temporary guards so that big events are covered without building every shift by hand

outcome: peak shifts are filled before the first wave of parcels
problem: Temps are added one at a time and the CSV import fails on small formatting errors.
scenarios: We bring on 300 people from Staffline in two weeks every October.
Adding them one at a time in the admin is a full week of work.
The CSV import fails if one phone number has a space.
New starters didn't get a rota because their accounts weren't ready.
statement: Parcel hub managers need to add hundreds of seasonal temps to the rota in a day so that peak shifts are filled before the first wave of parcels

outcome: nobody a client has refused is sent back to their site
problem: Client restrictions on individual workers live in managers' heads, so banned workers get rostered again.
scenarios: Calder Bank asked us never to send Pawel again and the rota put him there Monday.
Some buildings require vetting and only five of our cleaners have it.
Complaints about the same person keep coming back.
I keep a sticky note of who can't go where.
statement: Cleaning contract managers need to keep a list of workers each client has approved or banned so that nobody a client has refused is sent back to their site

outcome: paid hours match people actually on the floor
problem: Anyone can punch in from anywhere with someone else's PIN, so pay goes to people who aren't there.
scenarios: Caught a guy punching in four badges from the car park.
Our headcount on the floor is 60 and the clock says 67.
Some clock on from home, then drive in 20 minutes later.
Loss prevention says we paid 1,100 hours last quarter to people who weren't there.
statement: Warehouse operations managers need to stop workers clocking in for absent colleagues so that paid hours match people actually on the floor

outcome: a shift change doesn't mean a queue at the tablets
problem: Clocking in means typing a PIN on one of two tablets, which creates long queues at start times.
scenarios: At 6am there's a line of 80 people waiting at two iPads.
Everyone already carries an HID card for the doors.
Workers lose 7 minutes paid time each start waiting to punch.
Typing a 6-digit PIN with gloves on is a joke.
statement: Distribution centre shift leads need to let crews clock in by tapping their site badge so that a shift change doesn't mean a queue at the tablets

outcome: no worked time disappears
problem: Kiosks in freezer bays drop Wi-Fi and silently discard punches made while offline.
scenarios: The freezer bay tablet said success and then my Tuesday was blank.
Lost 3 hours on my pay; the supervisor says the system shows nothing.
Every week someone on nights has a missing in or out.
It shows a green tick, then later it's like I was never there.
statement: Cold-store workers need to have punches recorded when the kiosk loses connection so that no worked time disappears

outcome: their manager approves it instead of chasing paper forms
problem: Missed punches are corrected on paper slips that payroll keys in by hand.
scenarios: Forgot to punch out Friday; now I have to find the supervisor and fill a yellow slip.
Payroll fixes 300 missing punches a week by hand.
My timesheet shows 19 hours for one shift because I didn't punch out.
Let me just say 'I left at 6' in the app and the lead signs it off.
statement: Hourly workers need to fix a forgotten clock-out from their phone with a reason so that their manager approves it instead of chasing paper forms

outcome: the payroll cutoff is met every Monday
problem: Timesheets are approved site by site, so managers with dozens of sites miss the payroll deadline.
scenarios: I have 34 buildings and I open each one to click approve.
Monday 10am cutoff and I'm still clicking at 9:55.
Payroll gets late sign-offs and runs on estimates.
Exceptions I'd look at; the clean ones should go in one batch.
statement: Area managers need to approve a whole week of timesheets for many sites at once so that the payroll cutoff is met every Monday

outcome: they review a few dozen exceptions instead of thousands of timesheets
problem: There is no exception view, so odd punches reach payroll unless someone scrolls every timesheet.
scenarios: Every Monday I scroll 2,400 records looking for weird ones.
Someone had a 22-hour day and it went straight to ADP.
I want a list: no out, under 4 hours, over 12.
We find the problems after people get paid.
statement: Payroll supervisors need to see only the punches that need attention, such as missed, early or very long ones so that they review a few dozen exceptions instead of thousands of timesheets

outcome: break time comes off their hours correctly
problem: Breaks are deducted automatically or typed by leads, so recorded breaks rarely match reality.
scenarios: I take 30 minutes, the system takes 60 because the lead types it.
We write lunches on a clipboard by the canteen.
Auto-deduct takes a lunch even on days I worked straight through.
My pay is always half an hour short on doubles.
statement: Warehouse workers need to start and end unpaid breaks at the kiosk so that break time comes off their hours correctly

outcome: new starters are paid from their first hour
problem: Day-one starters cannot punch in, so their first shifts are missing from payroll.
scenarios: Day one temps don't have their login, so the first day is missing.
I write names on paper and HR keys them in later.
An agency guy worked a full day and didn't get paid for 3 weeks.
Let me punch someone in from my handset with a note.
statement: Shift leads need to clock in workers who have no phone or badge yet so that new starters are paid from their first hour

outcome: unplanned overtime is caught on the day
problem: Workers stay late without asking, and managers only see the cost in payroll.
scenarios: Pickers stay 40 minutes after to 'finish the trailer' and it adds up to £9k a month.
Nobody asked me if Tom could stay late; I see it on payroll.
I want the clock to ask for a lead's OK when someone punches out late.
Extra time is our biggest cost overrun and none of it is signed off.
statement: Logistics managers need to require approval before anyone works past their scheduled end so that unplanned overtime is caught on the day

outcome: they don't wait for a manager to start the shift
problem: Only managers can reset kiosk PINs, so workers who forget them can't punch in until a manager arrives.
scenarios: Forgot my 4-digit code and the manager doesn't arrive until 9.
Every Monday someone's locked out of the tablet.
The reset email goes to an address the worker doesn't have.
Make it text me a code.
statement: Kiosk users need to reset their own forgotten PIN at the kiosk so that they don't wait for a manager to start the shift

outcome: the attendance policy is applied the same way to everyone
problem: Attendance discipline is tracked in spreadsheets, so supervisors apply it inconsistently.
scenarios: Eight occurrences and you're out, and we keep the tally in Excel.
Two supervisors gave different warnings for the same lateness.
The union rep says we discipline unfairly and I can't prove otherwise.
I want no-call no-show to add 3 points automatically.
statement: HR managers at distribution centres need to track lateness and no-shows as attendance points so that the attendance policy is applied the same way to everyone

outcome: a missed visit is covered before the client goes without care
problem: Late or missed home visits only appear in next-day reports.
scenarios: Mr Patel waited 3 hours for his insulin call; we found out when his daughter rang.
I see missed calls on Monday's report, far too late.
If someone isn't at the door 15 minutes in, I want my phone to buzz.
Aides oversleep, it happens, but we need to know fast.
statement: Home care coordinators need to get alerted when an aide hasn't arrived at a visit so that a missed visit is covered before the client goes without care

outcome: early punches don't turn into paid minutes
problem: The kiosk accepts punches at any time, so arriving early becomes paid time.
scenarios: Drivers arrive at 5:30 for a 6:00 shift, punch in, and drink coffee on the clock.
15 minutes a day times 90 drivers is real money.
I want the kiosk to say 'too early, come back at 5:55'.
Payroll says we can't round it off, so stop it at the door.
statement: Depot managers need to stop people clocking in more than ten minutes before their start so that early punches don't turn into paid minutes

outcome: the agency can invoice and pay them without chasing paper
problem: Agency nurses carry paper timesheets that a ward manager must sign, and lost signatures delay pay.
scenarios: I still carry a paper sheet to every ward and chase a sister to sign it.
Lost signatures mean I wait a month to be paid.
The trust rejects sheets without the nurse in charge's name.
A photo of a crumpled form is how we send it now.
statement: Agency nurses need to get their timesheet signed by the ward on their phone at the end of a hospital shift so that the agency can invoice and pay them without chasing paper

outcome: lines restart on time after breaks
problem: Supervisors can't see who is still on break, so lines restart short-handed.
scenarios: Half the pack line wandered back at 10:47 from a 10:30 return.
I can't watch the canteen and the conveyor at the same time.
Want a ping on my handheld if anyone's out past 30.
We lose a pallet's throughput every afternoon to stragglers.
statement: Line supervisors need to know when someone's break runs long so that lines restart on time after breaks

outcome: return-to-work and sick pay follow the policy
problem: Sickness is shown on the rota as a grey block with no dates, notes or totals.
scenarios: I keep GP notes in a drawer and the time off on the rota as a grey block.
HR asked how many days Grace was off this year and I couldn't say.
Statutory sick pay was missed for two carers in May.
Back-to-work interviews never happen because nobody knows when people come back.
statement: Care home managers need to record sickness absence with the fit note attached so that return-to-work and sick pay follow the policy

outcome: chronic overstaffing or no-shows show up in one report
problem: Planned and actual hours live in separate exports, so variance by site is invisible.
scenarios: Plan says 1,200 hours at Daventry, payroll paid 1,410, nobody can explain it.
I build a pivot every Monday from two exports.
Which sites keep running over their rota? I can't tell.
The board wants rota accuracy as a KPI.
statement: Operations directors need to compare scheduled hours with worked hours per site each week so that chronic overstaffing or no-shows show up in one report

outcome: new starters don't get stuck on English prompts
problem: The kiosk is English-only and many warehouse workers misread it.
scenarios: Half my night crew is from Iasi and the tablet only speaks English.
People tap random buttons and end up on 'start break'.
Agency temps from Poland ask me to punch them in.
Could there be a flag to choose the language?
statement: Warehouse kiosk users need to use the clock-in screen in Polish, Romanian or Spanish so that new starters don't get stuck on English prompts

outcome: they can take paid days later instead of overtime pay
problem: TOIL balances are tracked on paper, so workers and supervisors disagree on what is owed.
scenarios: Our contract allows TOIL but we keep the balance on paper.
I did 14 more hours in December and want 2 days off in January.
Supervisors forget who's owed what.
HR spent a week reconciling balances at year end.
statement: Warehouse employees need to bank extra hours as time off in lieu so that they can take paid days later instead of overtime pay

outcome: the lead knows right away to find cover
problem: Calling in sick means phoning or texting a lead, and messages are missed until it is too late.
scenarios: I rang the depot at 5am, nobody picked up, then got marked no-show.
Calling in poorly means texting my lead's personal number.
Our sick line is a voicemail nobody checks until 9.
Want a button: 'can't make it' with a reason.
statement: Frontline workers need to report sick before a shift from the app so that the lead knows right away to find cover

outcome: evacuation roll calls account for everyone
problem: During an alarm, wardens use the printed rota, which does not show who actually came in.
scenarios: Fire alarm Tuesday; it took 25 minutes to check 140 people in the car park.
Our roll list is the printed rota, which is wrong half the time.
The insurer asked how we know nobody's left inside.
I want a list on my phone of who's in the building.
statement: Fire wardens at warehouses need to see who is clocked in on site right now so that evacuation roll calls account for everyone

outcome: a five-person crew isn't recorded as one person working
problem: Each cleaner must punch on their own phone, and many have no data, so only the leader's time is captured.
scenarios: We arrive as a van of five and only I have a phone that works.
Two of my team have no data plan.
I end up texting the office the names every morning.
Our timesheets show me on site and four ghosts.
statement: Cleaning team leaders need to clock in a whole van crew at once on arrival so that a five-person crew isn't recorded as one person working

outcome: client invoices match hours worked and get paid without disputes
problem: Billing is rebuilt by hand from several reports, so clients dispute invoices that don't match their sign-in books.
scenarios: Lakeside Tower disputes every invoice line because our numbers differ from their sign-in book.
I rebuild time per gate in Excel from three reports every month.
Our biggest customer is threatening to withhold payment until we show who stood where.
DSO is 78 days because invoices go out wrong.
statement: Security firm billing teams need to send each client a breakdown of guard hours by post so that client invoices match hours worked and get paid without disputes

outcome: workers' compensation premium audits are settled without overpaying
problem: Insurers audit payroll by job class, and Crewday cannot split hours and pay by classification.
scenarios: The insurer's auditor wants forklift drivers split from clerks; we can't.
We overpaid £31k premium because everyone got lumped in as warehouse.
Every February I lose a week to the comp audit.
Need a yearly file: class code, headcount, gross pay.
statement: Finance controllers need to report total hours and wages by job classification each year so that workers' compensation premium audits are settled without overpaying

outcome: driving between jobs isn't unpaid
problem: Only time at a client site is recorded, so travel between jobs is invisible to payroll.
scenarios: I do 7 houses a day and only the time inside counts.
My car does 400 a month for work and I see nothing for it.
Carers are leaving for supermarket jobs because the drive is free labour.
Our CSM keeps saying it's on the roadmap.
statement: Mobile field workers need to have time and distance between client sites counted in their pay so that driving between jobs isn't unpaid

outcome: carers' hourly pay never falls below minimum wage
problem: Gaps between home visits are unpaid, which pushes effective hourly pay under the legal minimum.
scenarios: An HMRC investigation found our staff dropped under the legal floor once the gaps were counted.
Twelve 30-minute calls with 10-minute gaps, only 6 hours paid.
We fudge it by adding a flat 15 minutes per call.
The tribunal case from a former carer is about exactly this.
statement: Home care payroll teams need to pay travel minutes between back-to-back visits as working time so that carers' hourly pay never falls below minimum wage

outcome: mileage is reimbursed from records, not guesses
problem: Mileage claims are filled from memory, so reimbursements are slow and unreliable.
scenarios: People fill in a form from memory at month end; some claim 200 a day.
I want the miles from their visits to land in Expensify monthly.
Our tax adviser says we need logs to back up the 45p rate.
Reimbursements are two months behind because I check every claim.
statement: Finance teams at field service firms need to export each worker's business miles to the expense system so that mileage is reimbursed from records, not guesses
who: Finance teams at field service firms

outcome: nobody rekeys hours and payroll runs without import errors
problem: Hours are exported as CSV, reformatted by hand, and uploaded to ADP, which introduces errors.
scenarios: Every other Thursday I download a CSV, fix the columns, and upload it to ADP.
ADP rejected the file because employee IDs had their leading zeros stripped.
One typo and 200 people get the wrong pay.
Our auditors flagged manual rekeying as a control weakness.
statement: Payroll administrators need to send approved hours straight into ADP Workforce Now so that nobody rekeys hours and payroll runs without import errors

outcome: premiums and differentials land in the right pay lines
problem: Crewday's pay codes don't map to UKG earnings codes, so premiums arrive as regular hours.
scenarios: Night premium shows up as regular hours in UKG, so 300 people were underpaid in June.
We maintain a 90-row mapping sheet between your codes and ours.
Ironvale's payroll lead said this is why they're evaluating Deputy.
Every new allowance we add means a ticket to your support team.
statement: Enterprise payroll teams on UKG Pro need to receive hours with pay codes mapped to UKG earnings codes so that premiums and differentials land in the right pay lines
who: Enterprise payroll teams on UKG Pro

outcome: unsocial hours are paid at the contracted rate
problem: Premiums are added by hand after export, and shifts crossing midnight are split wrongly.
scenarios: Carers who work Christmas Day should get double time; we add it by hand.
A shift crossing midnight gets all of it at the late rate, or none of it.
Our union contract says +18% after 10pm and the export ignores it.
Every pay run we have 20 corrections for Sunday work.
statement: Payroll managers need to apply night, weekend and bank-holiday premiums automatically so that unsocial hours are paid at the contracted rate

outcome: corrections reach the next pay run without reopening the whole period
problem: Fixing a closed period re-exports everyone's hours, causing double payments.
scenarios: A guard's Tuesday was missing; fixing it reopened the fortnight and resent 400 people's time.
We pay fixes by bank transfer and tidy the records later.
ADP double-counted after we re-exported a closed week.
I need a 'delta' file, not a full new export.
statement: Payroll teams need to correct hours after a pay period is closed and send only the difference so that corrections reach the next pay run without reopening the whole period

outcome: they can drop their separate payroll provider
problem: Small customers pay for a scheduling tool and a payroll tool and want one bill.
scenarios: Why do I pay Gusto AND you? Just do the whole thing.
My staff want payslips in the same app as their rota.
Tax filing would be amazing; then I'd cancel my bookkeeper.
A competitor bundles it in for £2 more per head.
statement: Small business owners need to run payroll and pay slips inside Crewday so that they can drop their separate payroll provider

outcome: an emergency doesn't push them to payday lenders
problem: Workers wait for a fixed pay date even when they have already earned the money.
scenarios: My car broke down Tuesday and we get paid on the 28th.

DailyPay keeps calling us about a partnership.
Could I see what I've made and take £100 now?
statement: Hourly workers need to draw part of their earned pay before payday so that an emergency doesn't push them to payday lenders

outcome: margin per placement is known before invoicing
problem: Bill rates and pay rates are kept in separate spreadsheets, so loss-making contracts go unnoticed.
scenarios: St. Bride's pays us £48 an hour for ICU, the nurse gets £31; I compute it in a spreadsheet.
